claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by electron-phonon coupling strength.
Atomic size mismatch modulates electron-phonon coupling strength in high-entropy alloys.
Increasing atomic size mismatch produces stronger local lattice distortions.
Stronger local lattice distortions enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering disrupts Cooper-pair coherence.
Disruption of Cooper-pair coherence lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
The baseline is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy whose similarly sized constituent atoms produce minimal atomic size mismatch.
Replacing one constituent with a significantly larger isoelectronic element increases atomic size mismatch while maintaining the overall electron count.
The larger atomic size difference increases local lattice strain and distortion.
Increased lattice strain and distortion alter the phonon spectrum.
The modified high-entropy alloy will have a lower superconducting transition temperature than the baseline alloy.
The proposed relationship applies when substitution is isoelectronic, introduces no additional magnetic moments, and causes no structural phase transition.
The proposed relationship is restricted to nonmagnetic-disorder regimes in which other electronic parameters remain largely unchanged.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling and disorder-related scattering may exert competing effects on the transition temperature.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis names electron-phonon coupling strength as the primary governor, but the operative causal mechanism attributes lower T_c to coherence-disrupting phonon scattering. The uncertainty field additionally suggests that electron-phonon coupling may be enhanced and compete with scattering, leaving the direction and role of the purported primary variable unresolved.
